I'll keep this short.

The concept of the singularity is the point at which the constraints on the rate of acceleration in technological progress don't vanish, but instead, change or reduce to some other variable or 'chokepoint'. It doesn't guarantee continued increases in computing power or machine intelligence, at all.

At the same time we are well on our way to sufficient computing power to simulate a human brain in an accurate neural model (more than five years, less than ten). What we lack is a broader understanding of what is going on in the brain at a systems level.

We can't build, let alone copy conscious, or even be sure the thing in question is conscious, without knowing concretely what consciousness is.

Look up the old ship of Theseus puzzle. You replace one plank in the ship. Is it the same ship? Replace a dozen planks? Still the same ship? Replace dozens more? And on, and on each time afterward, asking, is it the same ship? Until at last everything that was the ship has been replaced. Is it still the same ship?

Now what happens if you take all the old parts, and use them to build a new ship? Which is the true ship of Theseus?

Identity is more than just "I'm me. That thing over there is a copy!"

If you work off the assumption that 'you' are just the information contained and described by your brain, and not merely your brain alone (in the same way your operating system is not the same thing as your cpu or hardrive), then 'transferring consciousness' is certainly plausible.

And in the same manner, you may argue that consciousness arises from the brain, and is thus dependent on it, but dependence is not the same thing equivalence, e.x. your OS is dependent on a processor, but without one, it is just information--of course this is a poor metaphor because a few might argue the brain is not like a computer, and I could explain why they are wrong, but I'll leave that for another time.

My opinion? A copy is a copy. If you were to imagine the brain as a glass of water, and the opacity or transparency of the water as the information content, then the problem becomes clearer. Put a drop of ink in the first glass. Now take a second glass, fill it with water, and put a drop of ink in it too. The information content, in our simplified model, is the same. The one glass is a container with copied contents--the second cup is a dupe, with no causal relation to the other except for information content. The first cup could be shattered, spilled everywhere, just go on holding it's water, or even have new ink drops added--in this way, what happens to the first cup does not matter, in the same way copying the contents of a brain into a new brain or appropriate device, is not solved by killing the original host.

But suppose, bit by bit, we poured the contents of the first glass into the second glass, and replaced the missing water in the first glass, with fresh clear water. And we repeated this procedure until all the original contents were in a new form? In the end, if we replaced bits and pieces of the brain with hardware equivalents, allowing a mixing of new hardware, and old, along with new information and old information, it would seem the end result would not be a copy, but the original with a stable identity in a new 'container'.

Granted, all of this pales before a broader problem.

The real question is, are you conscious now? You can't answer for certain, because you don't know.

And without knowing what consciousness is, we can't definitely say it exists--and if it doesn't, if consciousness is just an epiphenomenon, emerging from a hodgepodge of other processes, then all of this is likely moot--because consciousness transfer will then rely on mapping all of those systems, and replacing those bit by bit, and that seems like a far vaster intellectual territory to conquer than the monolith we call 'conscious'.
